title: An Interview with Elder Jim Blizzard
speaker: Jim Blizzard (interviewed by unnamed moderator)
summary: In this interview format, Elder Jim Blizzard discusses his journey to pastoral ministry, his call to serve at Grace Church in Cape Canaveral, and his perspectives on the evangelical landscape, biblical sufficiency, and the challenges of balancing family and ministry. The conversation touches on his upbringing in a pastor's home, his evolution from initial reluctance toward ministry to answering God's call, and his vision for reaching younger families in an aging congregation.

outline.title: Personal Testimony and Background
subpoints: Growing up in a pastor's home with a lifelong trust in Christ
Witnessing pastoral hurt and initially resisting the call to ministry
Recognition of God's providence even through difficult circumstances

outline.title: The Call to Pastoral Ministry
subpoints: 2017 pastors conference highlighting the need for Bible-believing pastors
Recognition of the need for pastors engaged in their communities
Wife's supportive response and encouragement through seminary
Statistical decline in pastoral aspirations among seminary students

outline.title: Ministry at Grace Church Cape Canaveral
subpoints: Aging congregation with few young families
Geographic challenges with transient population
Deep commitment to God's Word among existing members
Grandfather founded the church over 40 years ago

outline.title: The Evangelical Landscape Today
subpoints: Growth of evangelicalism but in a watered-down form
Shift from cultural norm to cultural rejection of church attendance
Church hurt as a significant deterrent for young people
Importance of leaders practicing what they preach

outline.title: Denominational Identity and Distinctives
subpoints: Challenge of uncertain identity within the denomination
Known historically for what they are against rather than for
Need for positive affirmations beyond doctrinal denials
Reformed distinctives: biblical authority, pastoral care, confessional faithfulness, high view of holiness, literal creation understanding

outline.title: Personal Priorities: Family and Ministry Balance
subpoints: Challenge of time management with five children
Commitment that wife and children do not receive leftovers of pastoral care
Being a Christian must come before being a pastor
Intentionality required as children grow and leave home

outline.title: The Sufficiency of Scripture Under Attack
subpoints: Scripture is the foundational doctrine under greatest attack today

subpoints: Reaching younger families as primary goal

transcript:
## Opening Scripture Reading

> "And he himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists and some pastors and teachers. For the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry for the edifying of the body of Christ till we all come to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God to a perfect man to the measure of the Stature of the fullness of Christ that we should no longer be children tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine By the trickery of man and the cunning craftiness of deceitful plotting But speaking the truth in love may grow up in all things into him who is the head Christ From whom the whole body joined and knit together By what every joint supplies according to the effective working by which every part does its share Causes growth to the body for the edifying of itself in love." (Ephesians 4:11-16)

## Introduction

We are part of the body of Christ and that body goes beyond this local church. We're so thankful that Elder Blizzard could be with us today and that way remind us of our connection to the church in Cape Canaveral. We once had Pastor Cruz here in the afternoon and had a little interview conversation with him and a lot of people gave us positive feedback on that. So I thought we would do something similar with Jim. I asked if you would be willing to come and have a conversation about ministry, about calling, about churches working together, and so on.

## Personal Background and Testimony

### Longevity in the Church

Jim, you have been coming to this church since its conception. There are only three or four people in this room who have been here longer than you have.

Yes, that's correct. I've been part of this church since the beginning.

### Coming to Know the Lord

Tell us, how did you come to know the Lord? Did you grow up in the church?

Yes, I grew up in a pastor's home. It's been something difficult for me as an early child to describe my testimony because I don't remember a time when I didn't know Christ as my savior. That's not to say I've been saved since infancy, but I don't remember ever not trusting in Christ. Especially in early teen years I kind of struggled with that because I'd hear people give these fantastic testimonies about how God saved them from drugs and alcohol and this horrible life. In my mid-teens I came to the realization, talking with my father and others, that I could say the same thing—that God has saved me from all those things too—but I don't have to live with the consequences of those things.

Again, I don't remember a specific date and time that I prayed a sinner's prayer, but I can tell you that right now I am trusting Christ as my soul's salvation and I don't remember a time when that wasn't the case.

That's what we call a glorious testimony here at this church.

### Growing Up in a Pastor's House

How was it growing up in a pastor's house? We have some men here that might be interested in going into the ministry. They have children. How was that experience?

I shared some of this with others at lunch. I never wanted to be a pastor. I told my wife when we were dating that I don't want to be a pastor and have no desire to do that. Some of that came from seeing the hurt that my father had to go through from being a pastor—people leaving the church for ridiculous reasons. You know, the bowl got moved from here to there and that was the special bowl that person should have had and it should always be in that location. I got to see a lot of hurt on my father's side and I said I don't want that. I don't want that for my family.

But even through that, looking back I can see God's working and how God's used my father's life to be able to minister to other pastors who have gone through similar hurt. There's a great need for pastors. I read an article yesterday, I think by Pastor Dalma, asking whether the number of ministers in evangelical churches is shrinking. He came to the conclusion that it doesn't really matter if they are or not because God will provide for his church. But he uses means, and I'm a product of those means that he uses.

You've probably heard of NAPARC—the North American Reformed Protestant Church Council. It's a collection of fifteen Reformed denominations that represent about 1.4 million Reformed believers in North America. In those fifteen denominations, there are close to two hundred empty pulpits because they simply cannot be filled. Men are not aspiring to the ministry. Seventy percent of seminary students in seminaries that are serious about the Bible today are not on the pastoral track. They're doing seminary for some other reason.

So there's a great, great need. When I graduated from college in 2003, the vast majority of students who went through Clearwater Christian College with me were in pastoral studies majors. I think it was second only behind biblical studies. There were dozens of guys in pastoral studies. Now I've looked at some schools and it's maybe two or three people.

## The Call to Pastoral Ministry

### How the Decision Was Made

How did you come to the decision to pursue the pastorate?

It really started in probably 2017. I went to a pastors conference with my father—many of you know Pastor Blizzard. At that conference they talked about the need for pastors who believe the Bible and who will teach the Bible, and the reduced number of pastors today. They also talked about the need for pastors willing to be involved in their community as well—not just preaching on Sunday and that's all they do, but being active in our communities much like the Black Robe Regiment during the Revolutionary War.

I heard that and I thought, well, maybe this is something God wants for me. At the time I was working with an organization called Child Evangelism Fellowship, working with children in the public schools. That's a well-needed ministry. The vast majority of the kids there are not in local churches. It's a real struggle to get them to local churches, and part of the reason is because the local churches aren't teaching the gospel. There are a lot of churches out there that really are not a church.

So that kind of started that thinking. Then in 2018 we had Synod there in Lakeland. At the end of that time, a teacher said, "You know, you should take a seminary class on us." So I did—took theology to on the doctrine of God. Here I am eight years later. That's kind of what started that journey.

### The Conversation with His Wife

So when the Lord puts that in your heart, how did that conversation go with your wife?

My wife has a saying. Every time I come to her with something, if it's something biblical or something that's a hard ask but not necessarily outside the realm of scripture, she'll say, "Well, I'm not gonna stop you from doing that." I think that's probably what she said to me. When I said after I took that first seminary class that I wanted to continue on and keep taking classes, she said, "Well, I'm not gonna stop you. How can I help? I can't say no, right? You've got calling from God for this. I'm here and we'll support you."

And she has been a fantastic help to me. You can ask my professors. They know when my wife has proofread my paper and when she has not proofread my paper. There's a big difference there. You can ask Professor Lynch—her Hebrew pronunciation is much better than mine is. But she's been very supportive and very helpful along the way.

## Ministry at Grace Church

### About Grace Church Cape Canaveral

You have been ministering at Grace Church for almost two years now. Tell us about that church. Help us to know that church.

Grace is a very aging congregation. My children, the youngest of which is twelve, and we have two children in the congregation younger than mine. So with Sharon and Steve, our greatest need is for young families, which is difficult because of the area we're in. We have about nine thousand people in population in our city, and the vast majority of them are transient. It's not uncommon for us to have ten, fifteen, twenty visitors on a Sunday morning and every one of them going on a cruise. They will see you next on or next year. So it's difficult to try to get people to come here.

The transportation is different in Florida. I have to drive fifteen minutes to get to church and that's a long way. Which I understand is a very short time for the people at the Hunter's, I know. But yeah, and so that it's a challenge. I live on the mainland and then I cross a bridge to get to an island and I cross another bridge to get to another barrier island. That's where the church is, and to get people across those bridges is a challenge.

But the people who are there are very committed to God's Word and to the church itself. As you mentioned, my grandfather started the church just over forty years ago. So I have some relatives in the church—some aunts and uncles who were there. They were old when I was a teenager and now they're even older. But that's the majority of the congregation. And so I spend a lot of my time at the hospital and at doctors' visits with them. But they're like you—they love Christ and they want to see his gospel and his kingdom go forward.

### Location Benefits

I love that his church holds Synod because it's literally two city blocks from a sandy Atlantic Beach. So every break—no committee meetings for me. And if you go block the other direction, there's an ice cream cone right there, correct?

Yes.

So you split your time.

## The Evangelical Landscape

### Current State of Evangelicalism

You've been in the church for most of the last two years but in ministry for the last eighteen, twenty years really. How do you see the evangelical landscape from your perspective? What are the challenges and encouragement for the church?

It's really very split in my mind. I see evangelicalism as a whole growing but in a very watered-down way. When I was growing up, you'd ask somebody, "Do you know Christ?" They'd say, "Oh, yeah, I grew up in the church. I go to church now." There's very little of that now. It's not uncommon to hear, "No, I don't go to church. I don't want to go to church." It's very cool to not go to church right now. There's not that positive peer pressure almost to attend church.

But at the same time, there are a lot of people who have an understanding of scripture, an understanding of the gospel. Church hurt is a big thing these days, but it's odd to me because nobody says that about the gym or about the restaurant. You know, there was a server who was mean to me once and so I don't go back to restaurants.

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual for Psychiatric Disorders Six is coming up next year and one of the new diagnoses is religious trauma. RT's is going to be the next big diagnosis, along with climate change anxiety. The highest incidence of this is in the Pacific Northwest. It's very localized, and the people who are putting this together are saying this is a serious disease that people have. So anyway, yeah, it's hard to put the word "serious" and that together, but it is. At the same time, there are people who don't believe it. But it's long since become part of the diagnosis manual because it is viewed as a mental issue.

### Why Preach the Bible?

Why preach the Bible?

I mean, it's the only way by which man can be saved. And so we have to preach. "How will they hear without the preaching of the word? And how will they hear without a preacher?" How can the Bible pressure in church grow? That's an excellent question. That's above my pay grade, but if you want to graduate tomorrow, you're going to answer today.

Faithful training of the men of God through a biblical seminary.

### Practicing What You Preach

I think something that goes back a little bit to the church issue is that there have certainly been people in church who say one thing and do another. I think that's been a big deterrent for young people growing up—to see youth pastors and pastors and people in the church who say this is what you should do and then go out and live a completely different way.

It's very important that especially those who are in our church leadership practice what they preach. They live the same way that they say things from the pulpit. I think a big challenge for us as a synod, as a denomination, is that we are not too sure who we are. That's for certain. It's very difficult to go somewhere if you don't know where you're going because we don't know exactly what we are and what our distinctives are, right?

Well, I think I can tell you what our distinctives are, but I can also tell you all the exceptions that happened. It seems like for most of our history we've been known for what we are not.

Right, and that only should go so far. In order to have a winsome case for why people should get in the bus with you, you need to actually give them a positive—and when I mean positive, I mean what you are, not just what you are not. For me, denials are good, but you need some affirmations as well. And I think that's what we're missing.

I think there is in the big scheme of reformed churches a very necessary place for a person in a nation like us that takes the Bible seriously, that believes in pastoral care and counseling, that is confessionally faithful, and that has a high view of holiness and the idea of whom we associate with. I think there is a great and necessary place for a church that is also faithful to the scriptures in the sense of holding to a literal creation understanding of Genesis one and two. That's what I think we are. And if we can get that message clear out there, I think there are a lot of people that want to get on that bus with us.

## Personal Challenges: Family and Parenting

### The Challenge of Time with Children

You have five kids. What's your biggest challenge of raising kids?

Time. You only have so much time with your kids. And I'm quickly realizing that as my oldest is twenty and has moved out of state, and my next one is graduating and looking for what God has for him next. Just realizing I feel like I'm a parent to two kids these days because my twelve and fourteen-year-old are the only ones home. The older ones are working or out with friends. So making the most of the time with them and being very intentional about that, I think, is very important.

We had four under five and people say, "Oh, enjoy this time." Well, it's going to go fast. And if it'll allow you to enjoy drowning, then sure. But that seems to be a reality that actually is big.

### Marriage and Ministry Balance

This is a very intimate conversation for one of eighty people. What's a challenge in the ministry for marriage?

Yes, that's a real thing. Recently, one of the assignments I had to complete was to write out my philosophy of ministry and then defend it. The first point I put on there was that first I have to care for myself as a Christian before I'm a pastor. The second thing was that my children and my wife don't get the leftovers of my time. I have to care for them as I care for the flock, and even at least as good a straight away.

That's one of the things I would say is a challenge as well because it's not easy. But it's a whole lot easier to go, "Oh, I've got this phone call at ten o'clock at night. I've got to run down to the ER." But at the same time my wife is struggling with something. I go, "Well, I've got to deal with the church here. I need to go help these people here." And she can get the leftovers when it's done. And I think that same thing applies to children as well. So I think that's one of the biggest struggles—just to be able to manage my time properly so that way my wife doesn't get just the remnants.

## Biblical Doctrine Under Attack

### The Sufficiency of Scripture

What doctrine do you think is under the biggest attack today in your experience?

Probably it's got to be the sufficiency of scripture because everything else falls flat if you don't have that right. I mean, what is a man? What is a woman? Is it okay to murder infants in the womb? You know, all of that lacks a leg to stand on if we don't come back to the sufficiency of scripture.

The generation prior to ours dealt with the inspiration and inerrancy of scripture. It was a frontal attack by Satan. The debates on the authority and inerrancy are over. Satan is much more subtle now. He says, "Okay, yeah, you can have your Bible. Just don't think that it's good for everything. It's not sufficient. You need the Bible plus this other thing over here, and the Bible plus that other thing." And the church seems to be okay with that—that the Bible is the word of God, but it just doesn't apply to different parts of life.

Something that came out strongly in the introductory to counseling class is that scripture applies to all these areas. We don't need the Bible plus the DSM-6 to tell us how to treat these people. We need to treat the sin problem first, which we find in scripture.

## Vision for Grace Church

### Future Plans

Lord willing you get ordained May thirtieth. What's the first five years looking like?

Well, I've already told you the desire to reach younger families. So that's one of the big things. To establish a care system—the elders don't really have a structured care system right now for the current people. I'm looking to set that up first. We've already had some discussions toward that end. Really get that into place.

And then we've done some outreach. We've got a couple of people who are attending the church. We go out on the beach—it's only two blocks away—and invite people to church, witness to them. We've got one man who's there now that we're working through some significant issues with him, but he's coming to the church and very interested in the things of Christ. So branching out from there to try and reach not just individuals, or individuals only, but families. That's kind of the long-term plan.

## Serving as an Elder with His Father

### Honoring Your Father While Disagreeing

You served as an elder in the session when your dad was moderator. How was that?

It was difficult because I am not my father and I have very different views than he does. I had to be careful because not that I ever wanted to lie and pretend like I believed everything he did, but I wanted to honor him both as my father and as my pastor. So when I disagreed with him on certain things, I knew it sometimes would be difficult for him and hurtful for him. But I found ways to disagree in a kind way, in a way that he could understand the perspective I was coming from.

I think that's helped me in the session that I'm in now to address some of those who are much older than I and have been in the church more than twice my age, and be able to disagree with them in a respectful way as well.

Well, I appreciate you being willing to do that in the spur of the moment. And I hope that's a blessing for everybody to hear things like that and know how all the churches are doing and how their pastors are doing.
